def _acquire(self) -> None:
            ensure_directory_exists(self.lock_file)
            open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC
            if not Path(self.lock_file).exists():
                open_flags |= os.O_CREAT

This is exploitable only when (a) the process runs on win32, (b) an attacker can pre-create the lock path in a directory the victim process will use, and (c) the victim's process has write permission on the symlink target. Since the lock path is entirely caller-supplied (BaseFileLock.__init__ stores os.fspath(lock_file)) and filelock is a generic library used by privileged tools, the pattern is worth flagging, but the practical impact and prerequisites are unclear, so manual review is warranted rather than an outright true positive.

findings.description: Symlink-following file truncation in UnixFileLock._acquire (os.open with O_TRUNC and no O_NOFOLLOW)
findings.code_snippet:

findings.reasoning:
UnixFileLock._acquire() builds `open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC` (plus O_CREAT when the path is missing) and calls os.open() directly on self.lock_file without O_NOFOLLOW and without any lstat/symlink check. A grep for "NOFOLLOW" / "is_symlink" / "lstat" across the package returns zero matches, so nothing in this code path refuses to follow a symlink. The path existence check (`Path(self.lock_file).exists()`) itself follows symlinks, so it does not mitigate anything.

Because O_TRUNC is set and O_EXCL is absent, if an attacker can create (or pre-create) a symbolic link at the lock file path pointing to a file the victim process can write to, os.open() resolves the link and truncates the *target* to zero bytes. The lock path is fully caller-controlled (`FileLock(lock_file=...)` in _api.py stores os.fspath(lock_file) into the context), and lock files are commonly placed in shared/temporary directories (e.g. /tmp, shared caches, CI work dirs), which is exactly the scenario where a low-privileged local user can plant a symlink. The consequence is silent data destruction of an arbitrary victim file owned by the locking user, plus file-descriptor hijacking of the flock semantics (the lock is then taken on the attacker-chosen file). The correct fix is to add os.O_NOFOLLOW (when available) or open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL first and fall back to an fstat/fstat-vs-lstat inode comparison. Severity is low because it requires local write access to the lock directory and victim-writable target, but the data-loss impact is real.

The only guard is raise_on_not_writable_file(), which uses os.stat() (which follows links) purely to produce nicer errors, and ensure_directory_exists(). Neither rejects a reparse point.

Consequently, if a reparse point (symlink, directory junction, or hardlink to a same-volume file that the user can write) already exists at the lock path, the truncating open resolves it and zeroes the target file rather than failing. findings.description: SoftFileLock os.open with O_TRUNC — mitigated by O_CREAT|O_EXCL, cannot follow a pre-existing symlink
findings.code_snippet:
flags = (
            os.O_WRONLY  # open for writing only
            | os.O_CREAT
            | os.O_EXCL  # together with above raise EEXIST if the file specified by filename exists

findings.reasoning: The query flags O_TRUNC without O_NOFOLLOW here, but O_EXCL is combined with O_CREAT in the same flag word. That EEXIST is caught below and deliberately swallowed (treated as "lock already exists"), so no descriptor is obtained and no truncation of the symlink target can occur. O_TRUNC is therefore only ever applied to a file this call just created (and is dead weight). Symlink-following/truncation is not reachable in this path, so this CodeQL hit is a false positive.
